books.section: Topic 6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: J. F. Jarvis, 'Coxey's Army approaching Washington,' stereograph, 1894

stimulus.text: Stereograph photograph, “More Money! Less Misery! Good Roads!” Coxey’s Army approaching Washington, copyright 1894 by J. F. Jarvis. A column of unemployed men marches along a dirt road toward Washington, led by a man on horseback. Banners in the march read “More Money! Less Misery! Good Roads!” and “Death to Interest on Bonds.” The marchers set out from Massillon, Ohio, on March 25, 1894, and reached Washington on May 1 with about 500 men.
stimulus.source_note: J. F. Jarvis stereograph, copyright 1894, sold by Underwood & Underwood; Library of Congress, LC-DIG-stereo-1s09209. Public domain: photograph published 1894 (pre-1930). Banner wording checked against the image; march dates and numbers follow the standard account of Coxey's Army.

stem: Coxey’s Army reached Washington in May 1894, and its leaders were arrested on the Capitol grounds. What does the march best show about the Gilded Age debate over government?

options.text: Congress passed Coxey’s Good Roads bill at once
options.misconception: Congress never debated the Good Roads bill seriously, so it did not pass.

options.text: President Cleveland welcomed the marchers to the White House
options.misconception: Cleveland's administration prepared police and troops, and the leaders were arrested.

options.text: The marchers demanded lower tariffs on foreign goods
options.misconception: The marchers demanded federal jobs and more money, not lower tariffs.

options.text: Workers asked Washington for relief, while government still refused aid

rationales.A: Congress never gave the Good Roads bill serious debate, so it did not pass.
rationales.B: The administration met the march with police, and the leaders were arrested.
rationales.C: The marchers demanded federal jobs and more money, not tariff cuts.
rationales.D: The march asked Washington for jobs, and Washington answered with arrests, not aid.
rationales.general:
Weigh the ask against the answer.
1. Unemployed men marched hundreds of miles to ask Congress for work.
2. Their ask was new: the federal government itself should relieve unemployment.
3. The answer was old: police on the Capitol grounds, arrests, and no bill.
4. The march shows a new demand for federal relief meeting the old refusal to give it.
Remember: a protest's ending often shows which view of government still ruled.
